blocks.x: Russell collection.
Seven, ten, nine, eight. One, two, three, four, five. Okay. Really naturals, yogurt raisins.
See, then we're picking up. We're picking up now. Okay, now we got it. Okay. All right. You can, yeah, I think that's a good place.
Can't miss anything. Since I don't need any notes.
Well, if you have a dude, I've got a bunch here.
Thanks, but no thanks.
Okay. No, I think what I'm going to try and do first is start, maybe start with the Matassa family. We'll talk about the family.
Whatever you want. I mean, my time is your time.
Okay. Well, that's good. Okay, great. So I want to do.
I just can't stay over, but I mean, I can always come back.
Oh, yeah. Well, this is the first, the beginning, and we'll see where we get, how far we get.
All right.
I was wondering, why don't we start with your birthday?
Okay. Your birthday. I was born here in New Orleans. April 13, 1926.
Okay, 26. Okay, your father's name was?

Well, his name was actually Giovanni Cosimo. Cosimo. That's my, his middle name was my first name. Okay. And my grandfather was named Cosimo because that's the way that works sometimes. Firstborns are named after their grandfathers a lot of times. Anyway, he was John C. John Cosimo Matassa. He was born in Sheffaloo, Italy in 1895. Came to the United States in 1910. My mother was Dominica Leto, L-E-T-O. She was born in Palermo, Italy in 1902. Came to the United States in 1904 or 5. My father originally went to a small town in Mississippi where he had a job because in those days if you came to the United States you had to have a job, a suit and $50 in your pocket or something. The way it worked.
Do you know this for a fact or did somebody tell you this?

Well, my father, yeah. And so he went to work for an uncle in a little town in Mississippi called Chula, T-C-H-U-L-A, Chula, Mississippi. It's in the Delta. It's in the Delta. Yeah, not far from Jackson and Greenwood and like that. It was cotton country. Oh, okay. Especially in those days. Right. And in fact, he was there through World War I until right after World War I and there was a cotton crash. In fact, there's a blues song that talks about 10 cent cotton and 30 cent meat. Right. Yeah. Okay. And that's what they're talking about, right? Okay, sure.
It's peaking in the red.

Okay, it's peaking too much. All right. In the red. And he came to New Orleans where he worked for another uncle. Mm-hmm. Which... That was Vincent Matassa who had a grocery store in the French Quarter and who was a clarinetist. He played in...
No, he was also... He was a clarinetist.

Yeah. He played in the Italian association band. Wow. You know, they'd march on Saints Day, feast days and church things and stuff like that. In fact, my father was particularly proud of that day that he was a soloist. Something about being a soloist meant something to him in those days. Mm-hmm.
We've...
The nearest thing to what today would call a marching band.
So your father played?
No, my father didn't play. The uncle played. Just your uncle. Yeah, the uncle played.
Yeah.
And my father went to work for him, oh, I guess, in the 22, 21, something like that.
Mm-hmm.
And then he went to work for A&P, managing a little A&P store up on Magazine Street. By the time he was married to my mother, they were married in...
Yeah, what year?
Let's see. They would have been married in... 23, I guess. 1923, I'm... Yeah. And...
What church did you...
They got married by a justice of the peace in Mississippi.
Oh, well...

And that... And I'll tell you, for instance, how that kind of thing worked in those days. He got married, they eloped, went to the Mississippi coast, got married by a justice of peace, came back, and my mother, who had been raised devoutly Catholic, said, well, we should at least get the marriage, as they called it, blessed, which meant have a church ceremony. Sure. And they went to a priest that... I'm not sure, I think maybe what would have been St. Mary's, but it might have been St. Lucifer, but one of those two. In any event, the priest promptly informed my father, who wasn't... didn't hold the church in high esteem anyhow, that he wasn't married. And my father, being one of those absolutists, says, no, no, you got it backwards. If the state marries me, I'm married. If you marry me, I'm not married unless the state issues me a piece of paper saying that what you did was okay. Therefore, I'm married now, and I'm just going through this formality to please my wife. And the priest proceeded to argue with him about it, so he left, and he never had a church ceremony. Because my father just, you know, couldn't put up with that kind of stuff.
He seemed to be somewhat of a pragmatist.

Yeah, to a great extent. In any event, he moved to Dauphine and St. Philip Street and bought that business from a guy, William Tinker, T-I-N-K-E-R, who was retiring out of the grocery business. So that corner, Dauphine and St. Philip, 101 Dauphine, was probably a grocery since maybe the turn of the century.
Wow.

Before that, sometime before that, it had been an ice house, back when they used to bring ice cut from up north down on barges covered with sawdust and store it in houses and sell it that way. In any event, he came to Tenter, 101 Dauphine in 1924 and was there for many, many years. And that business went to two of my sons from my father because I was off in the music business, which he thought was a waste of my time. But that's another story.
Well, we'll get to it.
We'll get to it.
Yeah. We'll get to it eventually.

Okay. Yeah. He wanted me to take over the grocery store. I didn't want to. I didn't have anything against the grocery business, but I liked what I was doing better. And I, well, of course, I was born in April of 1926.
Now, were you, given your father's proclivity against the Catholic Church, were you baptized?
Yes, I was. Yes, I was. Oh, yeah. My mother prevailed on him. That had to be.
So, yeah.

Yeah, he relented. He would just teed off because the guy was trying to tell him what he knew wasn't right. And he's one of those guys you don't tell him when he knows something's right, or really believes it's right. You don't tell him it's wrong. Anyway, it was a minor blip in his lifetime, really, as far as he was concerned.
So, he brought in a major grudge against the Catholic Church?
No, no. In fact, he was usually pretty nice to him. Anyway.
What church were you baptized at?
St. Louis Cathedral.
Oh, because you all, was that your family church when you were growing up? You lived in the quarter?
Yeah, well, St. Mary's normally would have been. That was the Italian church. Yeah, but for reasons I don't know, my mother went to St. Louis Cathedral as a church.
But did you go there as a kid growing up?

Yeah, that's the school, that's the church I went to. That's where I was baptized, confirmed, all those things. Studied, you know, catechism in the after-hours classes because I went to public schools. I went to, actually, I started in St. Philip's School, the original school that's on the site of McDonough 15 now. Uh-huh. And then we were moved. I was maybe just in the first grade or so. I don't remember the exact year. We were moved to McDonough 15, which then sat on the grounds that are now empty at Barracks and Dauphine. Right. It was a big, empty lot there. And we stayed there until they built the new McDonough 15 in the early 30s and then transferred to there. So I went to McDonough 15 when it opened up for the very first time.
My point was that in those days, St. Louis Cathedral was a bit more residential. I mean, more of French Quarter people going to the cathedral rather than today.

Oh, yeah. It wasn't so much the church of the city, although it was the premier church. I really think that Holy Name of Jesus up here, but Loyola probably in those days was more the place where the archbishop and people like that had their things. The French Quarter in those days wasn't exactly looked upon the way it is now.
Yeah. I mean, it was more family-oriented.
Yeah. And it wasn't upscale.
Upscale. Today it's more tourist than others.
Right.
Upscale.
Yeah.
During those times. So you had to go to catechism classes on a special?
After school hours.
During the week?
During the week. During the week. I forget what days, but yeah.
And they would have certain days that you would go for kids who weren't actually in the
Catholic schools. In Catholic schools. Okay.
Because it seemed like that happened an awful lot. I think there was a more...
Yeah. Well, in those days, the public schools, most people went to public schools. There weren't nearly as many or as large, the Catholic schools.
So I think the Catholic church had to have more of these after-hours schools than I think that you went to.
Yes.
That there was more activity in that area. I went to start going through some of the city directories, and there's some matasses that I picked up in the...
Mm-hmm.
Going through the directories. And I... The first one I see in 1908 is a... Well, this may be a relative, but I don't know. It's a Vincenzo. Vincenzo.
Vincenzo. Vincenzo.
And it says Matasso. M-A-T-A-S-S-O.
That's because they mispronounced... It misspelled his name. They just misspelled it? Sure. That was my father's uncle, the one that he came to work...
That was his... Yeah.
Vincent Matassa, yeah.
Okay. That was the uncle. Mm-hmm. And interestingly enough, he's living at 527 Hospital Street, which became 527 Governor Nichols.
Right.
Which... Yeah. Which he would own.
Yeah.
At some point in time. In 1911, there's a Vincent Matassa, and he's working for the Lanassa brothers. And they have... They're at 1116 Decatur Street.
I don't know what that is. But, yeah, that's him. Yeah, that's him. That's still him. Yeah.
That's... But, and he's living... He's living on 1210 Charters.
Mm-hmm. Yeah, because Charters and Barracks is where the uncle's store was. So, it may be that...
In 1912, yeah, there's a Vincent... But they're spelling it Matasco. M-A-T-A-S-S-C-O.
Oh, well. Too bad.
So, it's always Matassa.
Yeah, sure. It's always been M-A-T-A-S-S-A. Okay.
Because I'm seeing all these different spellings in it.
Mm-hmm. For whatever it's worth, Matassa is the Italian word for skein, S-K-E-I-N. That's what it's called. You know, the loop of loose wool.
Okay.
Okay.
So, there's actual meaning there.
Yeah. Yeah. Well, most family names are. You know, Smith, obviously, being the most obvious one. And Baker, and so forth.

Mm-hmm. Let's see. There are a couple others. Yeah. Here, yeah. Vincent Matasso. M-A-T-A-S-O. He lives on Bourbon Street, and he's a musician. They list him in. This is 1918. He's listed as a musician.
Okay. He was a clarinetist.
Right. But did he...
But even primarily, he was a grocer.
But I'm going to... It seemed... You see, he lists himself here solely as a musician. So, I'm wondering if he's considering himself a... Trying to go professional, maybe.
No, not in that sense. Not far as I know. No. He didn't.
So, he always considered himself an amateur, basically, though.

Yeah. Well, I don't think people consider themselves amateurs or professionals in that sense in those days. It was purely what circles they played in that mattered. And it may be that that band played for fees or something. Well, yeah. I don't know that they didn't, you know. But, I mean, he wasn't a professional in the sense that that was his primary livelihood.
Okay. Now, 1926. 1926. Yeah, it's the first time I see John... John Matassa listed.
That's my father.
That's your father.
Yeah. What address they got for him there?
Yeah, right.
10-01-Dolphin.
Yeah. 1926. He'd been there two years by then.
And... And then, in 1931, there's a listing for... I'm going to... Giacomina?
Giacomina.
Giacomina.
Yeah, that was Vincent's daughter.
Oh, that's a daughter.
Mm-hmm. Vincent's daughter, yeah.
Vincent's daughter. And she's at 1234 Charters. Mm-hmm. And there's John, okay. Then Miss Mary.

Yeah, there was another daughter. And there was a John... John Jay was also a son of Vincent Matassa. My father was John C. So John Jay on Charter Street would have been the son of Vincent Matassa. And John Matassa on Dauphine Street would have been my father.
Okay. Let's see. In 1933... Yeah, there's a listing for... Yeah. John C. On St. Philip, 905 St. Philip.
Yeah, right. That's the other street.
There's a John C. 901 Governor Nichols. Which, I mean... And then there's a John Jay.
John... Well, John Jay is the one who was the... He would be my second cousin. He's my father's uncle's son.
Okay. And then Mary...
That's one of his sisters, yeah.
Okay. And then Vincent is living insurance. Mm-hmm. So that's... So that's... That's sort of the... Your father only had... Like, was there one... One brother?
One uncle here, yeah.
Are there other relatives, other places? Is there some in Mississippi? Do you still have relatives back in...
Well, he had another uncle in Mississippi. Right.
Who was?
That was Imaggio. He was actually my father's aunt's husband.
Oh, gosh. Okay.
Okay. All right. Okay. In other words, he was my father's uncle by marriage. Right. He's a guy my father first went to work for in Chula, Mississippi. And they lived at 637 Esplanade as Madjo's.
Okay.
Okay.
So did anyone ever give you any background on the family as far as why they came to America? I mean, was it just economic?
Economic. Pure and simple. Oh, absolutely. Yeah. Have no fear.
Oh, I don't know.
I mean...
Yeah.
I'll give you some...
No, if you have any stories.

Interesting side lights. And I don't guess enough people appreciate because it's happening today and people don't appreciate what it means. Of course, today they tell you for economic reasons, they don't want you to come to the United States. But, and that's only to hold the number down. But in Sicily, where my father lived, his father died. His father was a miller. His father died when he was 10 years old. And at 10, and I'm quite proud of this, at 10 years old, my father went and ran his father's mill and supported his family. And that came because obviously all you could do is eat out a living. They had a little plot of ground up on the hills where they raised some vegetables. The Italian name for that ground was Mangiafera. In Italian, that means eat iron. And it's so rocky and full of stones that literally it ate up plows and tools. And that's how it got its name, Mangiafera. Of course, you've got to remember, Italy's one big rock. There's not a whole lot of flat land or even arable land in Italy. So, yeah, he came to the United States pure and simple for economic reasons. And he had been studying in the craft system they have there, which meant he went to school in the morning and in the evening he was apprenticed to a shoemaker.
And he was learning to be a shoemaker.

And I remember him telling me that when he came to the United States, he'd only been here a short time. And some people had put out their trash to be picked up at the trash collection. And he noticed a pair of shoes being thrown away, a fairly decent pair of shoes. And as he told it to me, he says, where he came from, it wasn't unusual for someone to buy a new pair of shoes when they got married and be buried in that same pair of shoes. Yeah. Okay?
Yeah. Yeah.

You know, you had work shoes and you had a pair of dress shoes. And literally, you may buy one pair of dress shoes that lasted your entire life. Of course, the shoemakers liked that because they got to...
They kept reselling them.
Yeah, and repairing them. But he said he knew then he was in the right place. You know, you could do business in a country where people throw away perfectly good shoes. So...
So any stories of travels to this country, how they made it, how they got here?
Well, he came...
How he got the money, how he...

Well, he saved up his own money and came here. But he had to have this in writing promise of a job and a sponsor, in that sense, to be able to come. And in fact, if I recall, he got here... I don't know if the age was just 15 or 16, but below that age, he couldn't come on the paperwork that he was coming in. So they kept him in... So they kept him in... Literally, in jail at the immigration station. I think he arrived in Baltimore by ship. And they kept him confined for almost two weeks until he became 15 before they'd let him out. And he always called it... He always referred to it as the immigration jailhouse. Because that's what it was. Yeah, sure. And they called it being detained.
Well, I mean, there were a lot of... There was a lot of that. The Ellis Island, the stories from Ellis Island.
Yeah, same kinds of things. Same thing. Yeah.
I mean, your father just came a little bit later.
Yeah. Well, no, I think... It's a classic. Yeah. I think the bulk of the Italian immigration to this area had probably taken place by the time he came.
Yeah, by the time he came. Yeah. The real surge was in the 1880s and 1890s, which is what I assumed when your people came.

Yeah. That's what I assumed. Well, the other ones had been here before. You know, like I said, the Vincent Matassi had been here before. How much before my father, I don't know. But obviously, he was here... What did you find one in 1908? Yeah. Yeah, and he'd been here before. Yeah.
So... And he...

He had run a little shop along with his shoe repair in Mississippi. And that's... He developed his activity as a retailer, if you will. And that's all he ever did the rest of his life. Except for a little bootlegging.
How little?
Very little. He, you know, made a little wine that he sold in the store before liquor was...
But didn't every Italian do that?
Yeah. I was going to say...
Yeah.

Well, yeah. Prohibition wasn't exactly a popular law. It was acknowledged in its breach, if you will. And, yeah. The French Quarter was full of liquor. None of it legal, of course. Although I understood if you could get a doctor's prescription, you could always get scotch. The Kennedy family took care of that.
Scotch was the story.
Scotch was medicinal purposes? Yeah. The original... JFK's father...
Right.
...made his fortune originally by owning the rights to import scotch into the United States. Oh. And then got into real estate pretty heavy with the profits from the scotch.
But the way he could do it was that...
Yeah, well, right. There was a medicinal use of scotch.
Scotch had a medicinal use of...

So certain people, you know, always had a prescription for scotch. And I wouldn't be a bit surprised he sold a little bit under the table, but then who am I to impugn the family of the president, you know?
The Kennedy's. Were you born at home or in a hospital?
No, in a hospital. In a hospital. Hotel Duke.
Hotel Duke. Yeah. Hey.
Yeah.
So was I. There's always a problem with that when you tell people you were born in a hotel.
Hotel Duke, yeah. God's Hotel? Wait a minute. Pretty fancy place.
You know from out of town, think you were born in a hotel.
Yeah. Yeah.
You were born in a hotel.
I was an only child, I guess, after they saw me, they gave up.
Yeah, I was wondering. It would seem, you know, the Italians had...
Large families. Very large families.
And you were an only child.

Well, part of that was, again, religiously based. It wasn't religiously correct to do anything that's not have children. Mm-hmm. Supposedly that wasn't the primary reason you got married. Mm-hmm. Right. But, you know, one child. They had me.
Were you close to your other relative? Your cousin's relative?

Oh, yes. In fact, my mother's family had quite a lot of people who played music in it. Mm-hmm. And it had what amounted to a family band, you know. Her sister played, her sister played the, Chick Concetta played the piano. Concetta's husband played the clarinet.
What was his name?

He was Joseph DiGuardi. D-I-G-U-A-R-D-I. And, yeah. And I came up hearing Mazurkas and Polkas and Schottisches and Marches. Mm-hmm. I mean, Under the Double Eagle was a staple. Mm-hmm. And things like that. And, of course, I also heard them because in those days, the jazz bands on the street played them a lot more than they do now. And for some reason, those original things aren't played as much. When you go to a place now and listen to Dixieland or traditional jazz, you don't hear as many of those kinds of things as they actually played in those days. And I think it was because then they played primarily for people dancing. Right. Now they play in concert fashion and people sit and listen and it's a different milieu.
When would you hear the family play? When would you hear your relatives play?
Any occasion. That's births, deaths, weddings.

Okay, well, alright. I've got to finish doing now. I've got to take this thing. Alright, we forgot to billboard the last one. This is an interview with Cosmo Matassa. My name's Tad Jones, and it's May 28, 1993. This is reel number two, and we've got to go back and billboard reel number one. And we're at Tulane University at the Jazz Archive. Okay, that's out of the way. Okay. So, speaking of food, how was the food growing up? I mean, we think about people in New Orleans eating red beans and rice, and here's a big Italian family. Okay, wait a minute.

Two things you've got to remember. I came up as a small child during the Depression. I was fortunate enough for my folks on the grocery store. So I was spared the problems other people had. You know, what do we eat today?
Well, I mean, that was...

Yeah. So, in that sense, I was really lucky. I was very lucky. But there was not a lot of sharing, a lot of caring. Families tended to take care of family, that kind of stuff. And my father and mother, I know, on occasion did what they could to help somebody that they knew needed help. Right. Generally, the biggest single thing, and it seemed to happen regularly enough, as I became old enough to be aware of it, was people who were in very modest economic means having children, new babies. New babies. Right. That was always a time of joy, but also a real problem. And I can remember my mother being involved in that kind of stuff, you know, putting together a little package of stuff for somebody who just had a baby. And like I say, I was lucky. I didn't want in that sense. And although things were tough, food was, by today's standards, ridiculously cheap.
Wow.

And you've probably heard the old thing about Quatti beans. Maybe you haven't, I don't know. No, no. Tell me about it. For 10 cents. 10 cents? For 10 cents, you could go to the grocery store and get a little package of beans and rice, and a little black pepper and another piece of paper wrapped up like that, for a dime. You could get a piece of salt meat for 15 cents, a pretty big hunk of it. And what was that called? Salt meat, that's, it was called Quatti, which is a kind of half partial thing, you know, normally you would buy a pound of beans, but if you didn't have enough money to buy a whole pound, you could buy this lesser amount of beans and rice and be able to cook them in. And the red beans became famous for Mondays because Mondays was wash days. And red beans are something you could cook without having a stand and watch it all the time.
You just go over and stir it every now and then. Did you have standard food every, I mean, on this day was this meal, and this day was this meal?

Yeah, pretty much. Pretty much. Pretty much. It was generally that real meat dishes were sundae, roasts, chickens, and that kind of stuff, and always pasta. Right. You know, every meal had pasta. Always pasta. Yeah. Every meal had some kind of pasta. Oh. The main meal, the main dish of the meal. It was either a first dish or a side dish or whatever, depending on how it was fixed. And there were a billion ways to fix pasta.
But your mother knew how to do it.
Right.
But in those days you had to.

Yeah, right. Yeah, well, pasta was a staple. It was very inexpensive, good food. Yeah. In fact, most people don't appreciate it now. But a lot of dishes in those days were prepared because it was an entire meal in a dish. Stews, you know. All in one.
All in one.

All in one. Red beans and rice. Mm-hmm. Macaroni and meatballs. Mm-hmm. And variations on that. For instance, most of the fancier pasta dishes were really done in those days because a working guy could take it from home and have it for lunch. Mm-hmm. And it was everything in one thing, yeah. In fact, chicken cacciatore means hunter's chicken. Mm-hmm. Someone who's a cacciatore is going to go out and catch his things, right? It's a good cognate, in fact. Mm-hmm. Anyway, because it was a meal of the chicken and all the vegetables and all that the guy could take when he went out hunting. Mm-hmm. Again, one little pot and he had everything, that and bread, of course. And wine or beer, depending on whether you were Italian or Irish or Dutch or, you know. Everybody drank in that sense, I think. Just about everybody. But it was part of your meal. It wasn't, you weren't drinking in the sense of drinking. It was part of your meal.
Mm-hmm. So when are you first aware of, and I'm kind of know, I'm thinking of commercial music, more than- The jukeboxes.
Yeah. The jukeboxes, which meant I was aware of commercial music when I was seven years old. Mm-hmm. And you have to remember that in those days, although my father had a saloon, it was really two.
How do you mean?
It was segregated. There was a white saloon and a black saloon.
Okay.
So how was it- His arrangement was unique. Yeah. The wall between them had an arch, big enough for a wide door, and they built a phone booth into that.
Right.

So the telephone was accessible to either one. There was a door on each side of the phone. Right. Imagine a phone booth with a door on each side. Right. That's the way it was. And it was a jukebox in the white bar, and it was a jukebox in the black bar. So I got to hear country tunes, blues tunes, the whole thing, all that, yeah, because I heard them all.
Oh, so you're hearing like the standard pop songs of the day from the early 1930s.
Everywhere. Yeah. And I was hearing, of course, what black people listen to and what working class white people listen to at the same time. Yeah.
Any songs come to mind, things that you heard that stood out as a kid?

Well, yes and no. I can't now say this was the most impressive song I ever heard. But you've got to remember in those days I was hearing things like Lil Green, Ma Rainey, Armstrong of course, early Jordan, Louis Jordan. And of course on the other side I was hearing Bing Crosby, I was hearing the country artists, and people like that. And we always had one or two ethnic records on the white side, Irish tune or German tune, or depending on who was a regular customer that played the box a lot and said, why don't you get such and such and such, and I'd get it for them.
You know, that kind of thing. So, we talked about family. Were the Italian holidays very special for your family? Oh, sure. Yeah. I'm talking Columbus Day, St. Joseph's Day.

Well, there always were, yeah. There always were. My father was a work every day type, so there wasn't a lot of times when he would take off and participate. Right. But my mother and I and family would. And yeah, every holiday was important.
What was special about it? What was done differently on the holidays?

Well, different times, different things. For instance, you know, as you know in those days, it still is, but not in the same sense. But All Saints Day was a very, you know, you went out and cleaned and fixed up two of them and did something about that. And you also, you know, and everybody did.
Everybody did. I mean, you know, it was that kind of thing.
All of the other holidays, we, the rest of the holidays had to be the ones that were either national holidays or our version of it. For instance, in those days, it was, it was Decoration Day. Right.
That we, you know. Right.
Memorial, which is Memorial Day. Yeah. But it was a different day of the month. It was near the beginning of the month.
Well, that's right. It was early in May.

Earlier in May. Yeah. Yeah. Today we celebrated. Right. Memorial, Memorial, Decoration Day was Confederate Memorial Day in essence. And since the white power structure ran everything in those days, that's the one you celebrate. I didn't know why, but I mean, that's what it was.
And then the Memorial Day became more of a national holiday.
Yeah, right. And it became the national holiday.
Right. Which is what we celebrate. Right. It's the Decoration Day.
Birthdays were always important. Quite often you celebrate. Was it special for you?
Was that being an only child? Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. It was special because you got to go to other people's birthdays, which was a party. Oh, okay. Maybe music and cake and ice cream and food.
Any special Italian birthday different from the Italians doing the birthdays?

Any different? I don't recall anything that was peculiar to Italians in that sense of birthdays. Except Italians hug and kiss a lot more than some people do, you know what I mean? Everybody and anybody, you know.
Was that your family? I mean, were they?
Yeah, sure. Oh, yeah. For instance, as a child, when I was brought to somebody else, you know, you kissed all your uncles and your aunts and that kind of stuff. And my kids were brought up that way.
You know, not today.
Kids are, you're lucky if you can get a kid to say hello, you know. But .
I'm thinking of celebrations like, probably something you would remember is maybe your confirmation. Was that a big deal?

Oh, yeah. That was a big deal. You planned for that for weeks and weeks and it was a big deal. And you dressed in junior, you got a new white suit and you wore a big band with a ribbon thing on it and you held a gigantic candle with a ribbon on it and all. It was a big deal. And you graduated to what would be your adult prayer book and beads too, you know.
Did you march in a ceremony? Oh, yeah.

It was a very large group and you know, marched down the center and sat in a special place all together. St. Louis Cathedral. And then the archbishop would come down and everybody would be terrified of the archbishop. He represented some power. He didn't understand, you know.
St. Louis Cathedral? Must have been scary. Yeah.

Well, you know, kids didn't. And in those days the priests played games with reality, you know. You learned about the fact that the host was God's body and in those days as opposed to today, they would never put it in your hand. You know, you can go take communion now and they'll put it in your hand. They would never have allowed you to touch it with your hand. Gee whiz, no, no. And that sort of thing. And you were terrified you might drop it, you know.
Oh, yeah.
Oh, my God. It would fall out of your mouth. That would have been a disaster, you know. You'd be ruined for life.
So you're hearing music on the jukeboxes. What about radio?
Yeah. Well.
What stations are playing?
I don't recall what stations, I've got to be honest with you. But I remembered WDSU and WL, and there was another one that no longer exists. What the hell was it?
It was probably a mutual station, a mutual network.

And there were two, you know, the government split the NBC. They declared they had a monopoly. That's right. So there was a blue network and a red network of NBC. And I think the blue network is going to be in the ABC later.
But it seems to me there weren't as much music programming as there is today. I mean it was more.

Well, I think the single thing I remember most as a small child was the fact that very often Huey Long was on the radio. And that was an occasion. Let me tell you, the place would fill up. Because my dad would put a radio up in the bar and in the grocery. And the place would fill up. People would come to hear speeches by Huey Long. Huey Long. Huey had an enormous, enormous effect on people. In my remembrance of it. Absolutely. People looked on him like a savior. Oh. Yeah. History proves differently, but.
Well.
And he was a populist, you know, every man a king. Uh-huh. You can be a millionaire. Sort of like Clinton.
I think in a small way.
Yeah, in a small way. In a small way. He's going to pay your medical bills and tax the rich, you know.
In a small way. Right. To the radio, the radio wasn't as important as I think as live music was to you. I think as impressive, I think. Oh, no.

No. I don't think you would ever have considered anything but a second class substitute for live music. Live music was the defining thing. And luckily, McDonough 15, the public schools in those days had a good music program. Symphony players would come and demonstrate instruments, you know, in a little grammar school. You know, never do that today. You know, they might put on something and they'd haul 80 busloads of kids to an auditorium somewhere to hear them play or something. Right. And three or four of them would come and show you their instruments and tell you how they made and how they played and why they played that. And that happened in grammar schools in those days.
So you were in, which high school did you go to?
Warren Easton.
You went to Warren Easton.
It was a boys' high school then.
Didn't they have a music program? Oh yeah.
A great music program, yeah.
Yeah. I know you used to lay them. Big band.

In a lot of ways, it was like a mini LSU, Warren Easton. Same colors, purple and gold, and a big marching band. A great football team. When I went to Warren Easton in 1937 to 1941. I'll explain why in a minute, because if you figure that out, the arithmetic, I was pretty young.
I was going to say.

Yeah. But I went to Warren Easton in 1937 to 41. And in 1936, the year before I went to Warren Easton, in the regular season, the football team was undefeated, untied, and unscored on. Of course they went up to Baton Rouge and got beat by a Strumahe, bumped your big farmers, plowed up the field with them. But you know, those were days when Warren Easton had a fantastic athletic program. A very famous guy was the coach, Johnny Brechtel, who was really a good coach. He'd have been a professional coach by today's standards. A really good motivator, smart, and that kind of stuff. And he attracted kids. And then besides that, the public schools had a lot of kids that were very old still in high school. We had a couple guys on the team that were 21 years old, still playing high school football. And they were brutes. In 1937, because I remember this because it was so impressive, the line averaged over 200 pounds. You say, well that's not much, but wait, these were high school kids, okay? And they were huge.
It was fun. So how'd you get into Warren Easton at such a young age?

Well, when I was small, my mother used to, since she had to work in the store, she'd bring me down the stairs. In fact, as a baby, they'd put me in a wash tub. Oh, okay. And then sometimes customers had to watch me while my mother took care of working. But anyway, very early on, and I'm grateful till today that it happened that way. My mother used to take a cup and draw circles and draw lines and say, what time is that? You know, a short line, a long line. And she taught me to tell time. She taught me to count. She taught me my alphabet, how to spell my name, what my telephone number was. Because one of the important things was that if I was a small child and I got out somewhere, I needed to tell somebody what my name was, where I lived, what my phone number was. Okay. And so very small. I knew all that. I could do my alphabet back and forwards. And if they said M, I knew N was next and things like that. She played games with me, you know. She'd say P and I had to know Q was next and that kind of thing. So they also had kindergarten. It started normally around five in those days because you were in first grade at six. And I got put in kindergarten at four. And because I had all this home training, after I was in kindergarten for about two weeks, they put me out of it and put me in first grade because I was creating a turmoil with the rest of the kids. Because, you know, I knew all of this that these other kids were still trying to figure out, you know.
Or most of them.

There were a couple of, there was one little Jewish kid, smart kid, James Cohen. He had, he has a coin, an antique store on Royal Street today. His, his, his uncle was a Feldman who owned about three antique stores on Royal Street. They were well to do and I can remember they had, the family had a Pierce Arrow, big, like a touring car. Yeah. And they'd come pick him up after school with this huge Pierce Arrow. It was impressive. I tell you, I remember till today. It impressed me, I know. But, yeah, so, so I, I was in first grade at four. So I got out of the seventh grade. There was no junior high in those days. You went to the seventh grade and eighth grade was, it was high school. And so I got out of, uh, Warren East in 1937 at 11 years old. I went, I went to high school at 11.
That's, that's, that's very, yeah.

But, uh, a lot of, a lot of good things happened to me. I don't know if this is germane or what we're doing. Oh yeah, it is. Yeah, yeah, yeah. I'll just ride along. That, that, that my father's insurance agent, uh, was, was, uh, named Hirsch. Uh-huh. Henry Hirsch, the Jewish guy. And he had a friend, Marcus Korn, another Jewish guy who owned a plumbing company, Marion Plumbing Company uptown. And they used to take me to the, uh, Pelican ball games. Oh.
Okay.
And Henry Hirsch's wife always, as whatever occasion it was, she'd give me a gift. It was a book.
Oh, okay. Okay.

And, uh, and one of the things that, that she did, and I didn't realize it until I spoke to her about it later, was she gave me the entire Tarzan series by Edgar Rice Burroughs. Yeah, yeah. And it wasn't that she was interested in Tarzan, but she knew that Edgar Rice Burroughs was a, a good writer. Uh-huh. In other words, he, he, he wrote with good style and, and, and, and all those kinds of things. Yeah. So without me knowing it, I was learning the English language, enjoying reading the Tarzan series. Uh-huh. And, and, and, and a couple others she's getting, but then there was maybe seven or eight or 10 of those Tarzan books and I got them all. Uh-huh. But, you know, birthdays, Christmas, whatever. And, uh, another Jewish guy lived in the middle of the block named Rao, R-A-U. Uh-huh. And, uh, he owned an antique store on Royal Street. And, uh, he lived in the middle of the block and they were, they were, they had very kosher, uh, family style. They were Orthodox. Yeah, very. And, and, and, uh, I, I, you know, I used to go over there. They, they'd have me over for, for supper or something sometimes and, and that kind of thing. Just because we were friendly and in the neighborhood and all that. So I was exposed to some, some ethnicity. I wasn't that aware of what it was, you know. Uh-huh. Yeah. And in, and in those days you heard French and Spanish and Italian and German spoken on the street.
You heard, you heard, heard a lot of French and Spanish? Yeah. Uh-huh.

Because there were a lot of families still that first generation. And there was still a lot of times speaking there, you know, next door to me on St. Philip Street, it would have been about 907, St. Philip or 9, something like that, was a guy named Pruitt, P-R-O-U-E-T. And he was the second cook at, at, uh, Antwine's restroom.
Yeah.
And so I was exposed to that and he was a real Frenchman, I mean, you know. His wife was Constance and their daughter was Mion. And they, they exposed me to that side.
Uh-huh. Right. Both of my grandmothers spoke French. But that was that generation. Yeah. And it was the last generation that did that.
That's right. Yeah, nobody, nobody else did. My mother didn't.
No. Didn't take, take on. Uh, when you were young, when you were around the, the, the barroom and the grocery, did, did you, did you work at the grocery as a kid?

Oh, sure. That was another thing my father and mother taught me. Everybody works. So, as a, as a small child, when I came home in the evening from school, as a small child, I stacked soap on the lower shelf because I couldn't reach anything else. Right. I put soup up on the middle shelf and maybe, as I got taller, I put cereal on the top shelf. But everybody worked. Uh-huh. And I was, I was made to understand that, that you worked. Don't, never mind your daddy owns a grocery store. That has nothing to do with your life. Yeah, right. You work. And you understand why people work. So the work ethic. The work ethic was. The work ethic was there. Was there. There was no question about it. And in fact, it's, it was part of my life. Right. I didn't, I wasn't told this is the work ethic. Uh-huh. I lived it. You knew it. I lived it. Yeah. Which is a, maybe part of the problem with the work ethic. Is we need to quit calling it work ethic and just live it.
Uh-huh. But anyway, uh.
It's not enough of it.
No.
And, uh, so, so, and, and again, even though it was a grocery store, I could not go help myself to candy or a soft drink.
Uh-huh.
I got candy after dinner if I hadn't messed up that day, you know, and I had a soft drink with dinner again if I, if I hadn't messed up that day.
Speaking of messing up, what, what did that mean, messing up? What, what did you do?

Oh, oh, little, little things. I remember as a small kid, probably one of my, another one of those basic character building things, I hope this part of my character was, they dug up the street to do some kind of repair, and of course all in, all in New Orleans is all that clay, you know. Oh, yeah. So myself and a couple of my little school buddies, we discovered this mound of clay, and we immediately started to have fun with it, which meant making little balls of clay and throwing them stick on the wall of the building across the street. Yeah. And my father came out and everybody split and left me, right?
Well, of course.

Sure. So he, he got me a ladder and a bucket and a rag, and I cleaned the clay off the wall. And I'm crying, but I didn't do it all. He says, no. He says, but I caught you. You know what I caught. Isn't that the way?
Yeah. So was your father overall very strict with him? I mean, just in general?
He was strict in the sense that, you know, that you did things the right way, you know, the way you worked on it.
Right way, the wrong way, and his way?
Yeah. Oh, no, no. He, you know, he, well he was good about explaining to me why something was done this way, and not that way. Right. That kind of thing. No.
No question about it.

And my father, of course, since it was a depression, he worked all the time. He owned a little pickup truck, Model A Ford pickup truck. And on weekends, because people moved a lot, couldn't pay rent, they'd move in with a relative until they could get a job and move back out again. And he moved families on weekends with that little truck and made extra money with that. Uh-huh. Oh.
So that was, so he, Jack of all trades kind of guy?

Sort of, yeah. Yeah, he also would pack his little black bag with eight or ten sets of dice and a pistol and some folding money and go out to little towns and run crap games in the back of stores and things like that. Well, that can be dangerous.
Yeah, it could be. That's why you take your gun.

I was about to say. But, and he made a few bucks that way, you know? And then later on, he and a partner owned a little illicit gambling house. When gambling was taking place in Araby and had the big gambling house there, illegal but obviously public. Right. There were several smaller ones operating along, I think that's Friscoville Avenue, the street that runs from St. Claude to the river that it was on. And my dad and a partner had a little gambling house, if you will, a little place in a little double house that had little walls taken on the other side of it. And so I got to learn about gambling early on. The guy who ran that place was pretty much an expert gambler. And he showed me what to look out for, which is why I never became a gambler because...
So you had to run the game or to watch out for the...

Well, how it worked, for instance. There were catalogs of layouts of dice tables. You know how to, you know, you bet on this, you bet on these odds here and that. And in those catalogs was a description of the odds versus the payoffs. In other words, you could get one layout that was a little more liberal than another. You know, and that kind of thing. And so I was aware that it was a highly structured business. It wasn't a game of chance.
As in how to stack the deck against someone? Well, no.

Against someone? I mean, how to... This may... You may find this interesting, but it was so that gambling houses had to learn about how people cheat to protect themselves. And the gambling houses didn't cheat. They didn't need to. If you stayed there and gambled, you lost. It was... It's built into the system. You cannot win. Now, that doesn't mean that occasionally some fools don't win for a little while. Right. But you cannot win. The long... In fact, they had these little chants that you say, the guys would scoop up the dice and return them back to you. They had a little chants that they'd take that literally taunted you. You know? And I remember one until today, because it rhymed. And the guy would scoop up the dice and send it back to you and says, if you stay, you got to go. The longer you stay, the further you go.
Right.

Yeah. Meaning, I dare you to throw the dice out and put some money on the table, I'm going to beat you. And if you do it twice, I'm going to beat you twice. If you do it ten times, I'll beat you... You know, that kind of thing. And there were names, you know, all the names for the dice came up. Little Joe and Craps and Four and Eight, the Hard Way, meaning you only got two identical numbers. All those kinds of things. A lot of them I don't remember anymore. And also, how cards were marked.
Okay. For instance.

And the evolution of crooked dice. Listen to this. The original crooked dice were what's called loaded dice. And what they were, were tiny little gold pellets put in the paint. You know, they'd dig out to make the numbers, one here, two there. Right. So, they'd be little gold pellets. So, that side tended to lay down, so the thing on the other side would come up. So, loaded dice was the original thing. Well, the gambling houses, if they suspected somebody using loaded dice, all they had to do was pick the dice up and drop them in a glass of water. And they would...
Right. They would come up and...

They would literally turn around. They'd belly up. Right. So, then they started making them that they, one side was very slick and the opposite side had more friction. And they would tend to go along and flip over easier one way than another. Or that they were geometrically imperfect. They weren't perfect cubes. Okay. And things like that. So, I learned all about things like that and how cards were marked and all that. But it was because the gambling houses had to protect themselves from the clientele. Most people think it's the other way around and it isn't. They don't have to cheat you. Believe me. You just stay there and play. They got you. You know. And...
So, when you're at... Was Mr. Valentino at Warren Easton then? No.
When you were at Warren Easton? No.
After. Maybe he was after. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. What's his first name? He became legendary at Warren Easton. Yeah. But I think he was there after you. Maybe he went to Warren Easton.
Could he have gone there at the same time? He may have. I don't recall that. I didn't know him in that sense then.
Okay.
Because I was there from 37 to 41, like I say.
Warren, you were obviously a good student.

Well, I was... I lived a disciplined life and I was an only child, so I didn't have any choice. You know. And of course that made a difference. I came up here. You know. I was 15 years old and I came to Tulane.
Yeah. And they told me that I had to wait until I was 16.
I was 16.
Mm-hmm. And which I did.
Mm-hmm. And what did you study?

This is the thing. I came to Tulane to be a chemist. A chemist? Yeah. I signed up in arts and sciences and I took the scientific majors and that kind of stuff. Mm-hmm. And by the time I was here two years and really knew what a chemist was, I didn't want to be
a chemist. Mm-hmm.
And shortly thereafter, I was going to be old enough, 18, to be drafted. World War II was going on.
Right.

And so we were having trimesters in those days because the government was in a hurry to get new soldiers. They had three semesters a year, so they called them trimesters. Yeah. And it was a very brief break between them. Mm-hmm. And so you could do a year and a half in a year. Yeah. Because you made three sessions. Yeah. Yeah. And so it was a big drag, you know, a lot of work. And in January of the year I was going to be 18, I told my father I didn't want to register for the winter season, the winter session, because I was probably going to get drafted and I deserved a little time off. And he went along with that.
He said, okay, you know.

But the war in Europe ended. I had poor eyesight and a hammered toe, so I didn't get drafted. Mm-hmm. And he told me, well, good Italian kid, you've got to either work or go to school, you have no choice. Okay. And he owned a half interest in a little jukebox business.
Okay.

And since I had by now determined that I didn't want to be a chemist and I didn't know what I did want to be, I said, well, let me go work on a jukebox trial. And that's what happened. I went to work on a jukebox trial. Okay.
The tape's almost about to run out.
Okay. We'll. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Oh, I understand that. Okay. Okay, well, now reel number three. Reel number three with Cosmo Matassa. Cosmo Matassa? Yeah. And it's still May 28, 1993. Okay. So we're up to the- We're up to the-

segments.title: Opening and plan to start with the Matassa family
segments.summary: Recording set-up chatter; the interviewer proposes starting with family history.

segments.title: Birth and parents' origins in Italy
segments.summary: Matassa gives his birth date and his parents' names, birthplaces and emigration dates.

segments.title: Father in Mississippi cotton country, then to uncle Vincent's grocery
segments.summary: His father worked for an uncle in the Delta until the cotton crash, then for Vincent Matassa, a grocer and clarinetist in the Italian association band.

segments.title: Parents' elopement and the priest who said they were unmarried
segments.summary: His parents married before a justice of the peace; a priest later disputed it and his father refused a church ceremony.

segments.title: The Dauphine and St. Philip grocery and the father's wish that he take it over
segments.summary: His father bought the corner grocery in 1924; Matassa went into music instead, which his father thought a waste.

segments.title: Baptism, St. Louis Cathedral and early public schools
segments.summary: His mother prevailed on baptism at the cathedral; he went to catechism classes and to St. Philip's and McDonough 15.

segments.title: The Quarter's character then and catechism for public school children
segments.summary: They discuss the French Quarter as a family neighborhood and after-school catechism for public school pupils.

segments.title: City directory spellings of the Matassa name
segments.summary: The interviewer reads directory listings for Vincent Matassa and variant spellings; Matassa explains the name means skein.

segments.title: Uncle Vincent listed as a musician but really a grocer
segments.summary: Vincent was a clarinetist but an amateur in the sense that grocery was his livelihood.

segments.title: More Matassa relatives in the directories
segments.summary: They identify his father, Vincent's children and an uncle by marriage in Mississippi.

segments.title: Why the father emigrated: poverty in Sicily and the thrown-away shoes
segments.summary: His father ran his dead father's mill at ten, apprenticed as a shoemaker, and saw America's wealth in discarded shoes.

segments.title: The father's immigration, detention and retail career
segments.summary: His father was held almost two weeks at the immigration station until old enough, then worked in retail.

segments.title: Bootlegging, Prohibition and Kennedy scotch
segments.summary: His father made a little wine in Prohibition; talk drifts to medicinal scotch and the Kennedys.

segments.title: Born at Hotel Duke, an only child
segments.summary: Matassa was born in a hospital, a hotel, and was an only child.

segments.title: Mother's family band and the music he grew up hearing
segments.summary: His aunt and her husband Joseph DiGuardi played piano and clarinet; he heard mazurkas, polkas and marches at family occasions.

segments.title: Reel two opening; Depression food, red beans and cheap groceries
segments.summary: Reel two is announced, then Matassa explains growing up in a grocery during the Depression and how cheap beans and salt meat were.

segments.title: Italian meals, pasta and one-pot dishes
segments.summary: Every meal had pasta, and many dishes were whole meals a working man could carry.

segments.title: Jukeboxes in the segregated white and black bars
segments.summary: His father's saloon was two bars with a shared phone booth; he heard blues, country and pop on both jukeboxes from age seven.

segments.title: Italian holidays, Decoration Day and birthdays
segments.summary: Holidays, All Saints Day, Confederate Memorial Day and birthday customs in an Italian family.

segments.title: Confirmation at St. Louis Cathedral
segments.summary: His confirmation, the archbishop and childhood fear of the host.

segments.title: Radio and Huey Long speeches in the bar
segments.summary: He recalls radio networks and crowds gathering to hear Huey Long; radio was no match for live music.

segments.title: School music programs and Warren Easton High School
segments.summary: Grammar school brought symphony players; Warren Easton had a band and a famed football team, 1937-41.

segments.title: Mother's home teaching and starting school at four
segments.summary: His mother taught him time, letters and numbers, so he skipped through first grade and entered high school at eleven.

segments.title: Jewish and French neighbors, Tarzan books and languages in the Quarter
segments.summary: Neighbors and his father's insurance agent's circle shaped him; French, Spanish, Italian and German were heard on the street.

segments.title: Work ethic: stocking shelves and growing up in the grocery
segments.summary: Everyone worked; he stacked shelves, earned candy by behaving, and was punished for throwing clay.

segments.title: His father's strictness and the Model A truck
segments.summary: His father explained the right way to do things and moved families on weekends in a pickup truck.

segments.title: Father's crap games and gambling house
segments.summary: His father ran dice games in country stores and had a small illicit gambling house where Matassa learned how it worked.

segments.title: How gambling houses guard against cheating, loaded dice
segments.summary: Matassa explains why houses need no cheating, dice chants and the evolution of crooked dice.

segments.title: Mr. Valentino question; being a good student and entering Tulane at 15
segments.summary: A question about Valentino at Warren Easton, then Matassa's disciplined upbringing and arriving at Tulane at 15 or 16.

segments.title: Tulane chemistry, the draft and going to work in the jukebox business
segments.summary: He studied toward chemistry, left school before the draft, was not drafted, and went to work on a jukebox route.

segments.title: Tape running out and start of reel three
segments.summary: The tape change and announcement of reel three.
